statement: Between 1:00 pm and 5:00 pm on the same afternoon, how many times do the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock make an angle of exactly $90^\circ$?

choices.misconception: I counted only the times when the minute hand is a quarter turn behind the hour hand.
I counted only the times when the minute hand is a quarter turn ahead of the hour hand.
I counted two right angles in each of the four hours and then added one more for 3:00.
I assumed the hands make a right angle exactly twice in every hour.

hints: How much faster than the hour hand does the minute hand turn?

Track how far the minute hand has gained on the hour hand. A right angle happens each time that gain passes a quarter turn or three quarters of a turn, counted around and around. Watch the moment 3:00.

The minute hand gains $330^\circ$ every hour, so $1320^\circ$ in four hours. At 1:00 it is $30^\circ$ behind. Right angles happen whenever it is $90^\circ$ behind or $90^\circ$ ahead; one of these falls exactly at 3:00.

solutions.reliable: The minute hand turns $360^\circ$ an hour and the hour hand $30^\circ$, so the minute hand gains $330^\circ$ every hour on the hour hand. Measure the angle from the hour hand forward to the minute hand. At 1:00 it is $330^\circ$, and by 5:00 it has grown by $4 \times 330 = 1320^\circ$ to $1650^\circ$. A right angle happens when this angle is $90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$ more than a whole number of turns: $450, 630, 810, 990, 1170, 1350, 1530$. That is 7 times, and the one at $990^\circ$ is exactly 3:00. The hour from 2:00 to 3:00 and the hour from 3:00 to 4:00 share that single right angle, which is why the count is one less than 8. The transferable idea: count events by how much one hand gains on the other, and watch for an event that lands exactly on a boundary.
solutions.elegant: In 12 hours the minute hand gains 11 full turns, giving 22 right angles, not 24, so some hours contain only one. Listing them: about 1:22, 1:55, 2:27, 3:00, 3:33, 4:05 and 4:38.

whyOnTest: Clock problems are relative motion: counting right angles needs the gain of one hand on the other, and the trap is assuming two per hour.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
